title: Iris and the Data Adventure
markdown:
Dawn broke. Colours exploded. Sunbeams painted Iris’s room. Birds made a thunderous song of it. Today was the Elmwood Civic Science Fair. Iris sprang up, heart thumping. Her mission: why were Elmwood’s pollinators vanishing?

Her workbench was a disaster. Piles of numbers, insect counts, dates — a jumbled mess. Comet, her lurcher, nudged a stack. Papers cascaded.

“Comet, no!”

He wagged, a happy whirlwind. “This is bad,” she groaned. The data swam. How could anyone understand this chaos? Bees from March in one heap. Hoverflies from last Tuesday under a mug. A page of moths that had acquired a paw print.

A brisk rap-tap-tap. Ranger Elowen stood there, wide smile. “Looks like a data tangle.”

Iris gestured at the paper explosion. “It’s just numbers. So messy. I can’t see what’s happening.”

Elowen bounded inside. “These numbers tell us something. We just help them shout.” She led Iris to a table bathed in sunlight and handed over a ruler and vibrant pencils. “Let’s draw their story.”

She took the bee counts. “What if we made a little bar for each week? Taller if more bees, shorter if fewer.” She sketched quickly. Bars shot up, dipped. Comet watched, tail thumping. Soon a staircase of colourful bars stretched across the page. Not just numbers. A picture. A dramatic drop.

“Wow,” Iris whispered. “A mountain range. Going down fast.”

“You’re seeing the trend. That’s the point of making the numbers visible.” Elowen’s voice brimmed. “Now — which pollinators are disappearing most?” She showed Iris how to cut slices from a circle, like a pie. Each slice an insect type. Iris plotted. The pie showed a shocking truth: the buzzing bees were now just tiny slivers. Hoverflies held more of the plate than they used to, which was not comfort. It was a vacancy with better PR.

Fueled by understanding and a less romantic urgency, Iris and Comet worked at speed. Comet held papers down. Iris plotted more graphs, a line for moths that wobbled, a bar for beetles that stayed almost honest. The jumbled numbers became a visual story. The decline was not a statistic. It was stark.

At the Science Fair she unveiled the display. A hush moved through the buzzing crowd. The colourful graphs did the shouting without anyone calling them magic. Elowen stood beside her and kept it practical. “These charts let you see a drop you could argue with on a spreadsheet. Harder to argue with a mountain going down.”

People nodded, faces serious. Someone asked about the empty hive behind the library. Iris pointed to the week the bee bar collapsed and did not smile about it.

She looked at her graphs, purpose bubbling, bittersweet as the missing hum. She did not declare the day. She packed the raw counts under the pictures so a sceptic could check the bones, scratched Comet’s ears in apology for the cascade, and sharpened the pencil for the next week’s bar, which she hoped — without promising — might not be shorter.
